newsitem.title: GREECE: FOCUS - Possible new FRN tax unsettles Greek market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Possible new FRN tax unsettles Greek market.

text.p: Greek financial markets were in jitters over a a debate on whether the government, desperate to drum up new revenues, will impose a withholding tax on the coupons of outstanding FRNs, bankers said.
The focus of the debate is whether the government would use the gross 12-month T-bill yield or the lower after-tax yield in fixing coupons of existing three, five and seven-year floaters.

"The loss of market confidence will be the first negative outcome of a decision not to use the gross 12-month T-bill yield in resetting coupons on outstanding FRNs," Marinos Yannopoulos, executive general manager at private Alpha Credit Bank told Reuters.

Greek FRN coupons are reset using the benchmark 12-month T-bill and a spread over it. The current spread on the popular seven-year FRNs is 150 basis points. Banks also hold outstanding three-, five- and seven-year FRNs carrying larger spreads.
Yannopoulos said that the government was running the risk of reversing the downward trend in real rates that Greece has been experiencing in the last two years.
Real interest rates on government paper have come down to around four percent from nine to 10 percent a few years ago.
Other senior bankers said that the spectre of a sell-off from foreign and domestic players holding FRNs would become a reality if the government essentially taxed coupons.
"Upheaval. This is the word that describes what is going to happen if coupons are taxed," said a treasurer at a foreign bank. "It is not going to be just foreigners that will unload."
The government has yet to take an official position publicly on the issue of taxing state securities for individual holders for the first time.
Some officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said it was clear that new issues of securities would be taxed but no decision had been taken on existing floaters.
The socialist government is preparing its 1997 budget, which is due this month, and is striving to meet its revenue targets.
A high-level national economy official told Reuters that the government was leaning against taxing outstanding FRNs but the final decision was still pending.

The local press has reported the government will impose a withholding tax of 8.0 percent on interest earned from state securities by individuals. Interest income from state securities is already being taxed when bought by mutual funds, insurance companies and corporations.
Bank deposits already have a 15 percent withholding tax. A high-level central bank official told Reuters income from financial products should be taxed to remove market distortions.

"All incomes from financial products should be taxed in the same way to avert market distortions," he said. "This does not mean that a 15 percent withholding tax should be levied at once. A lower tax rate can be introduced the first time around."
The official declined to say whether he favoured the resetting of FRN coupons to be based on a gross or a net 12-month T-bill yield.
But with hundreds of billions of FRNs placed abroad the mere thought of fixing the coupons on the basis of net 12-month T-bill yield has sent shivers through financial markets.
Dealers estimated the minimum amount of FRNs placed abroad at 450 billion drachmas and a maximum of more than 1.0 trillion drachmas.

"The market is nervous. We have already seen some major foreign players reducing exposure on the circulating tax rumours in the last two working days," said a foreign bank bond trader. "I just hope they (government officials) do not make the mistake."

Greece issues primarily three-, six- and 12-month T-bills as well as three-, five- and seven-year floaters. The market has been swamped by rumours that the treasury will issue three or five year discount bonds by the end of the year.

"I bought this paper because it was stated in writing that it was tax-free and offered an attractive yield," said a London-based bond trader. "Now I am hearing they might tax them. How does it strike you?"
Other London-based foreign dealers said portfolio switching would follow the imposition of a tax and would lead to some kind of short-term volatility.

"A tax will prompt portfolio switching and lead to short-term volatility in which case the prudent behaviour is to abstain," said a London-based bond trader. "In my view, the upside is priced in but the downside is unlimited."
Greece has bilateral treaties with Britain and other countries and will end up paying the price anyway, he said.

Analysts and dealers have said the bilateral treaties left the door open to arbitrage and the tax experiment could prove very costly meaning tax revenues could be outpaced by higher interest payments.

A good chunk of FRNs purchases by foreign players had been funded via the ecu route and there was concern that a potential FRN sell-off would lead to huge forex outflows and an ensuing liquidity squeeze that would drive money rates higher.

The state also would end up paying a higher price on its paper as local banks weary about the impact of the revaluation of bond portfolios on their balance sheets after a tax would shed future auctions of state securities.

"Do you think we will be as aggressive as before the tax when we know that foreign clients are not willing to buy the paper and our bond portfolios would have been hit by the higher rates?," asked a dealer. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
